passages.happening:
Psalm 146 begins the last five psalms of the book. Each of them begins and ends with “Hallelujah!”, ‘praise the LORD’. This one turns to the singer's own soul. “Hallelujah! Praise the LORD, O my soul” (verse 1). “I will praise the LORD all my life; I will sing praises to my God while I have my being” (verse 2).

Then a warning. “Put not your trust in princes, in mortal man, who cannot save” (verse 3). “When his spirit departs, he returns to the ground; on that very day his plans perish” (verse 4).

The better trust is in God. “Blessed is he whose help is the God of Jacob, whose hope is in the LORD his God” (verse 5), the Maker of heaven and earth, who “remains faithful forever” (verse 6).

Then comes a list of what this God does. “He executes justice for the oppressed and gives food to the hungry. The LORD sets the prisoners free” (verse 7). And “the LORD opens the eyes of the blind, the LORD lifts those who are weighed down, the LORD loves the righteous” (verse 8). “The LORD protects foreigners; He sustains the fatherless and the widow, but the ways of the wicked He frustrates” (verse 9). “The LORD reigns forever, your God, O Zion, for all generations. Hallelujah!” (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
The book page says that many readers take these five psalms, 146 to 150, as the close of Book Five and of the whole book. It also says that Psalms 145 to 150 are part of Jewish morning prayer every day.

‘Princes’ means rulers: kings, nobles, anyone with power. Verse 4 gives the reason not to lean on them. They die. The Hebrew of verse 4 plays on the word for ‘ground’, adamah, from which ‘man’, adam, was made (Genesis 2:7). Rulers go back to the dust, and their plans die with them.

This warning applies to every ruler and every party alike. No modern leader or group is in view, and none is exempt.

Notice the list in verses 7 to 9. These were the people with no one to speak for them in the ancient world: the oppressed, the hungry, prisoners, the blind, foreigners, orphans, widows. A good king was supposed to protect them. Princes often did not. The LORD does.
passages.later:
Psalm 118 had said it already: “It is better to take refuge in the LORD than to trust in princes” (Psalm 118:9).

When John the Baptist asked whether Jesus was the one to come, Jesus answered with a list like verses 7 and 8: “The blind receive sight, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, and the good news is preached to the poor” (Matthew 11:5). James wrote that true religion is “to care for orphans and widows in their distress” (James 1:27).
passages.asks:
Where are you placing your hope: in a leader, a party, a person with power? Psalm 146 does not say they do not matter. It says they cannot save, and that they will die. Only God remains faithful forever.

And look at the people God cares for in verses 7 to 9. If you belong to him, they are your concern too.
